quests.instruction: Find the first place where one word runs into the next
quests.textToSpeak: I'll call Alex after lunch
quests.hint: This sentence has two links. Say it at normal speed and choose the one you hear earlier.
quests.explanation: Say 'call Alex' and the dark /l/ stays on your tongue while /æ/ begins, so the voice carries straight on. The sentence also links 'Alex after', through the final /s/ of 'Alex'. A fluent speaker joins both, which is why the question has to say which one it wants.
quests.flowRule: Thought groups: Fluent speakers connect words across a whole phrase, so one sentence can contain several links. The instruction tells you which one to find; listen to the sounds on each side of a boundary.

quests.instruction: Which is the last connection in this sentence?
quests.textToSpeak: drop the kids off at eight
quests.hint: Say the sentence at normal speed and mark each link. Take the one nearest the end.
quests.explanation: 'Kids off', 'off at' and 'at eight' all connect, so the end of the sentence is one chain of sound. The last link puts the /t/ of 'at' onto the /eɪ/ of 'eight', and the time arrives as a single unit rather than 'at… eight'.
quests.flowRule: Thought groups: Fluent speakers connect words across a whole phrase, so one sentence can contain several links. The instruction tells you which one to find; listen to the sounds on each side of a boundary.

quests.instruction: Which link sits in the middle of the sentence?
quests.textToSpeak: ask about each option
quests.hint: Every boundary in this four-word sentence is a link. Which one has a link on both sides?
quests.explanation: 'Ask about', 'about each' and 'each option' all join up. The middle one is the /t/ of 'about' running into the long vowel of 'each'. Hearing the whole sentence as one unbroken ribbon matters more than isolating a single pair.
quests.flowRule: Thought groups: Fluent speakers connect words across a whole phrase, so one sentence can contain several links. The instruction tells you which one to find; listen to the sounds on each side of a boundary.

quests.instruction: Find the link that runs on a hum (m, n or ng)
quests.textToSpeak: she's an only child
quests.hint: Hum through the sentence slowly. At one boundary the hum rolls straight into a vowel.
quests.explanation: The weak /ən/ of 'an' keeps your voice humming through the nose into the /əʊ/ of 'only'. The other link, 'she's an', is carried by a /z/, which you can also hold, so the two are easy to confuse. Ask whether the sound is made through the nose.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (nasals): A word ending in /m/ or /n/ keeps your voice running, so the nasal sound flows directly into a following vowel with no gap.

quests.instruction: Find the link where a stop sound meets a vowel
quests.textToSpeak: I got an offer
quests.hint: A stop sound closes the mouth completely for an instant and then lets go. Which word ends like that?
quests.explanation: 'Got' closes on /t/ and releases it straight into the weak /ən/, while 'an offer' is carried by a nasal instead. The stress falls on 'got' and 'off', so the little 'an' gets squeezed between them.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Find the link where a held sound like s, z, f or v flows into a vowel
quests.textToSpeak: this week is absolutely packed
quests.hint: 'Week is' also links, but through a different kind of sound. Choose the one you can hold for as long as you like.
quests.explanation: 'Is' ends in /z/, a sound you can sustain, and 'absolutely' starts with /æ/, so the buzz simply runs on. 'Week is' links through a /k/ stop, so it is the wrong type for this question. Holding the sound keeps the sentence fluent.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (continuous sounds): Sounds you can hold, such as /s/, /z/, /f/, /v/ and /ʃ/, glide directly into a following vowel without restarting.

quests.instruction: Which link goes into a word with a silent h?
quests.textToSpeak: it's an honour to meet you
quests.hint: Look at the first letter of each word that follows a short article. One is not pronounced the way it is written.
quests.explanation: In 'honour' the h is silent, so the word begins with a vowel and 'an' links straight into it. That is also why we say 'an' here rather than 'a'. 'It's an' links too, but only the silent-h link depends on sound rather than spelling.
quests.flowRule: Silent 'h': In words like 'hour', 'honest' and 'honour' the written h is not pronounced, so the word begins with a vowel sound and links to the word before it (and takes 'an', not 'a').

quests.instruction: Spelling can mislead: which pair really connects?
quests.textToSpeak: get one at the store
quests.hint: A number word looks as if it starts with a vowel. Say it slowly: what is its first sound?
quests.explanation: 'One' is spelled with a vowel but starts with /w/, so 'get one' is a consonant meeting a consonant and does not link. The real link is the /n/ of 'one' running into the weak /ət/. Spelling can suggest a link that the sounds do not support.
quests.flowRule: Sound, not spelling: letters that look like vowels can start with a consonant sound (the u in 'useful' is /j/, the o in 'one' is /w/), so no vowel link is available there. Linking depends on the sound a word really begins or ends with.

quests.instruction: Ignore the spelling: which pair connects?
quests.textToSpeak: it's a useful tip
quests.hint: 'A useful' looks like two vowels in a row. Say 'useful' slowly and listen to how it starts.
quests.explanation: 'Useful' begins with /j/, as in 'you', so 'a useful' is a vowel followed by a consonant sound and there is nothing to link. The /s/ of 'it's' running into the weak /ə/ is the real connection. Do not let the letter u decide for you.
quests.flowRule: Sound, not spelling: letters that look like vowels can start with a consonant sound (the u in 'useful' is /j/, the o in 'one' is /w/), so no vowel link is available there. Linking depends on the sound a word really begins or ends with.

quests.instruction: Which link attaches a weak little word to the word before it?
quests.textToSpeak: keep it open all day
quests.hint: Little grammar words lean on their neighbours. Which of the three links ends in one?
quests.explanation: 'It' is unstressed here, so it hangs on to 'keep' and the /p/ lands on its vowel. The other two links, 'it open' and 'open all', go into the stressed words 'open' and 'all', which carry more weight.
quests.flowRule: Weak Function Words: Short grammar words such as a, an, of, at, and, or and it are normally unstressed and begin with a vowel sound, so they attach to the word before them.

quests.instruction: Which link lands on a content word rather than a grammar word?
quests.textToSpeak: they stopped at eleven
quests.hint: One link goes into a tiny word you barely hear; the other goes into a number you hear clearly.
quests.explanation: 'Stopped at' links into the weak /ət/, but 'at eleven' gives the /t/ a full word to land on, and 'eleven' is the information the listener needs. Links into content words are often easier to catch than links into grammar words.
quests.flowRule: Weak Function Words: Short grammar words such as a, an, of, at, and, or and it are normally unstressed and begin with a vowel sound, so they attach to the word before them.

quests.instruction: Which link closes the sentence?
quests.textToSpeak: I need a bit of advice
quests.hint: Count from the end: which link comes last?
quests.explanation: 'Of' is /əv/, and its /v/ lands directly on the /ə/ that starts 'advice'. Phrases like 'a bit of' behave as one reduced chunk, which is why all three links in this sentence are easy to miss.
quests.flowRule: Reduced forms: Unstressed to, and, of, at, it, us and a shrink to /tə/, /ən/, /əv/, /ət/, /ɪt/, /əs/ and /ə/, so a link into one of them sounds like the end of the word before it.

quests.instruction: Which link carries the past-tense ending?
quests.textToSpeak: she worked on it all night
quests.hint: Find the verb in the past tense. Its ending is a /t/ you might be tempted to drop.
quests.explanation: The -ed of 'worked' is pronounced /t/, and it lands on the vowel of 'on'. Without that /t/ the sentence would sound like 'she work on it', present tense. 'On it' and 'it all' link too, but they carry no grammar.
quests.flowRule: Past-tense endings link too: A final -ed (/t/ or /d/) joins a following vowel, which also keeps the past-tense signal audible.

quests.instruction: Which pair links even though the first word ends in a silent e?
quests.textToSpeak: give us a minute
quests.hint: Say the first word of the pair without thinking about its spelling. What does it really end with?
quests.explanation: 'Give' is spelled with a final e, but what you say is /v/. That /v/ runs into the /ʌ/ of 'us'. 'Us a' links too, but it starts from /s/, not from a silent letter, so only 'give us' matches the question.
quests.flowRule: Linking follows sound, not spelling: a silent final 'e' (as in 'give' or 'close') does not block a link, because the word really ends in a consonant sound such as /v/ or /z/.

quests.instruction: Only one connection here is real. Which pair?
quests.textToSpeak: I was just asking
quests.hint: 'Was just' meets /z/ and /dʒ/. Look for the word that ends in a cluster before a vowel.
quests.explanation: Here is a cluster link: 'just' finishes with /st/, then 'asking' starts with a vowel, so the /s/ (and the /t/ if you say it) flows on. 'Was just' is a consonant meeting a consonant, so it stays separate.
quests.flowRule: Linking after consonant clusters: When a word ends in two or three consonants, the last one still connects into a following vowel, so the ending is carried across the boundary smoothly.

quests.instruction: Which is the second link in this sentence?
quests.textToSpeak: I'd like to return an item
quests.hint: Mark every link as you say the sentence, then take the second one.
quests.explanation: 'Return an' and 'an item' form a short chain: the /n/ of 'return' lands on the weak /ən/, and its /n/ lands on the /ɪ/ of 'item'. The question asks for the second link, but in speech the two are one flowing line.
quests.flowRule: Thought groups: Fluent speakers connect words across a whole phrase, so one sentence can contain several links. The instruction tells you which one to find; listen to the sounds on each side of a boundary.

quests.instruction: Find the link carried by the sound /l/
quests.textToSpeak: this jacket is on sale until Sunday
quests.hint: There are three links. Only one is carried by a sound you make with the tip of your tongue on the ridge behind your teeth.
quests.explanation: 'Sale' ends in /l/ and 'until' begins with /ʌ/, so the tongue stays raised while the vowel starts. 'Jacket is' and 'is on' link through /t/ and /z/ instead. Shop signs are often read quickly, so this link tends to be smoothed over.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (/l/): A word-final /l/ stays voiced and slides into the vowel of the next word, so the two words sound like one continuous stretch.

quests.instruction: Which pair has a weak grammar word joining on?
quests.textToSpeak: it comes in an extra large
quests.hint: Of the three links, which one attaches a tiny grammar word to what comes before it?
quests.explanation: 'An' is a weak /ən/, so the /n/ of 'in' leans straight onto it and the pair sounds like one short beat. 'Comes in' and 'an extra' go into stressed words. Size labels are said fast, so the weak link is easy to lose.
quests.flowRule: Weak Function Words: Short grammar words such as a, an, of, at, and, or and it are normally unstressed and begin with a vowel sound, so they attach to the word before them.

quests.instruction: Which link is released from a stop (p, t, k, b, d or g)?
quests.textToSpeak: the bus arrives at about ten
quests.hint: 'Bus arrives' and 'arrives at' link through held sounds. Which link is released from a stop?
quests.explanation: The /t/ of 'at' closes the mouth and then releases into the weak /ə/ of 'about', so you get one run of sound. The two earlier links use /s/ and /z/ instead, which you can hold, unlike a stop.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Which link has a nasal sound meeting a vowel?
quests.textToSpeak: I'd like an aisle seat if possible
quests.hint: Nasal sounds keep the voice going. Check each word's last sound: which one is nasal and followed by a vowel?
quests.explanation: 'An' keeps the voice running on /n/ into the /aɪ/ of 'aisle', where the s is silent. 'Like an' and 'seat if' are carried by stops, so the nasal link is the one that sounds smoothest.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (nasals): A word ending in /m/ or /n/ keeps your voice running, so the nasal sound flows directly into a following vowel with no gap.

quests.instruction: Which link is carried by a sound you can hold?
quests.textToSpeak: get off at the next stop
quests.hint: 'Get off' also links. Choose the link you could keep humming on as long as you liked.
quests.explanation: Hold the /f/ of 'off' and let it fade into the weak vowel of 'at'; that is the whole link. 'Get off' links through a /t/ stop instead. Passengers say this line quickly, so the held sound helps it come out as one phrase.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (continuous sounds): Sounds you can hold, such as /s/, /z/, /f/, /v/ and /ʃ/, glide directly into a following vowel without restarting.

quests.instruction: Find the link carried by a 'ch' or 'j' sound
quests.textToSpeak: please attach an invoice and a receipt
quests.hint: A 'ch' or 'j' sound ends one word. What does it meet?
quests.explanation: After the 'ch' of 'attach', the weak vowel of 'an' follows with no pause. The later links, 'an invoice', 'invoice and' and 'and a', come in a row, which makes the whole request sound like one flowing phrase.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (affricates): The 'ch' sound /tʃ/ and the 'j' sound /dʒ/ at the end of a word are released directly into the next vowel instead of being cut off.

quests.instruction: Which link begins with a stop sound?
quests.textToSpeak: I'll finish it after lunch
quests.hint: 'Finish it' links too, but through a sound you can hold. Which link starts with a stop?
quests.explanation: The /t/ of 'it' lands on the /æ/ or /ɑː/ of 'after', depending on accent, so 'it after' flows as one chunk. 'Finish it' uses the held /ʃ/, so it is the wrong type for this question. 'After lunch' has no link: /r/ or a weak vowel meets /l/.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Find the link that keeps a past-tense -ed audible
quests.textToSpeak: Sam asked if anyone had an update
quests.hint: Find a verb in the past tense. Its ending is a /t/ or /d/ that attaches to the next word.
quests.explanation: The -ed of 'asked' is a /t/ and it lands on the vowel of 'if', so the past tense stays audible. 'If anyone', 'had an' and 'an update' also link, but none of them carries the verb ending.
quests.flowRule: Past-tense endings link too: A final -ed (/t/ or /d/) joins a following vowel, which also keeps the past-tense signal audible.

quests.instruction: Which pair is joined by a nasal sound?
quests.textToSpeak: thanks for having us over
quests.hint: Rest a finger lightly on your nose while you speak: one boundary buzzes straight into the next word.
quests.explanation: 'Having' ends in /ŋ/, a hum made at the back of the mouth, and 'us' begins with a vowel, so the voice never stops. 'Us over' links through /s/. Hosts hear this phrase constantly, and warm delivery depends on that smoothness.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (nasals): A word ending in /m/ or /n/ keeps your voice running, so the nasal sound flows directly into a following vowel with no gap.

quests.instruction: Find the link where a stop sound meets a vowel
quests.textToSpeak: let's get everyone a drink
quests.hint: A stop closes the mouth for an instant and then releases. Which release lands straight on a vowel?
quests.explanation: The /t/ of 'get' releases straight into the /e/ of 'everyone', and the sentence carries on with 'everyone a'. Offering a round of drinks is said briskly, so the stop is released rather than held.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Find the final link
quests.textToSpeak: he's an old friend of mine
quests.hint: Listen to the very end of the sentence. The last link is the one the question wants.
quests.explanation: 'Of' is the weak /əv/, so the /d/ at the end of 'friend' lands directly on it and the pair sounds like one word. The earlier links, 'he's an' and 'an old', set up a rhythm that carries to the end.
quests.flowRule: Reduced forms: Unstressed to, and, of, at, it, us and a shrink to /tə/, /ən/, /əv/, /ət/, /ɪt/, /əs/ and /ə/, so a link into one of them sounds like the end of the word before it.

quests.instruction: Which pair is joined by a 'ch' or 'j' sound?
quests.textToSpeak: the match is about to start
quests.hint: Find the word whose last sound is like the start of 'church' or 'judge'. What follows it?
quests.explanation: Say 'match is' without a pause and the 'ch' is released directly into the vowel of 'is'. 'Is about' links through /z/ instead. Match announcements often run these words together at speed.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (affricates): The 'ch' sound /tʃ/ and the 'j' sound /dʒ/ at the end of a word are released directly into the next vowel instead of being cut off.

quests.instruction: Find the link carried by a 'th' sound
quests.textToSpeak: both of us were nervous
quests.hint: A 'th' sound ends one word. What does it meet?
quests.explanation: The breathy /θ/ at the end of 'both' keeps the airflow going into the weak /əv/. 'Of us' links through /v/. The weak, weak, stress rhythm of the sentence helps the phrase flow.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (/θ/ and /ð/): The 'th' sounds at the end of a word stay in the airflow and connect to a following vowel instead of stopping.

quests.instruction: Find the link that runs on a hum (m, n or ng)
quests.textToSpeak: I'm out of milk and eggs
quests.hint: Say the candidates with and without a pause. The nasal link is the one that sounds odd when split.
quests.explanation: 'I'm' ends in /m/, so the lips are closed and the voice keeps humming into the /aʊ/ of 'out'. The later links 'out of', 'milk and' and 'and eggs' use stops, so only the first is a nasal link.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (nasals): A word ending in /m/ or /n/ keeps your voice running, so the nasal sound flows directly into a following vowel with no gap.
